extracted.intended_audience: patent attorneys, EPO applicants/agents, examiners, and IP litigators working on European patents
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on how claims should be interpreted in EPO pre-grant and opposition proceedings, including the role of the description and drawings and the applicability of Articles 69 and 84 EPC. Useful for drafting claims and assessing novelty/ inventive step and scope during prosecution and oppositions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims are the starting point for patentability assessment
rubrics_metrics.description: The claims are the starting point and the basis for assessing the patentability of an invention under Articles 52 to 57 EPC.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing novelty, inventive step and other patentability requirements, begin from the claim language itself as the primary reference. The claim text establishes the matter for which protection is sought and provides the baseline for evaluation, even though other sources (description/drawings) will be consulted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Description and drawings must always be consulted when interpreting claims
rubrics_metrics.description: The description and any drawings are always referred to when interpreting the claims, and not just in the case of unclarity or ambiguity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contrary to some prior EPO practice, examiners, opponents and patentees should consult the description and figures in every claim interpretation exercise in pre‑grant and opposition proceedings. This aligns EPO practice with national courts and the Unified Patent Court and aims to harmonise interpretation across stages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Article 69(1) EPC (and its Protocol) concerns patent effects/infringement, not patentability
rubrics_metrics.description: Article 69 EPC is found under 'Effects of the European patent and the European patent application' and in particular pertains to infringement and should therefore not be construed as a definitive basis for assessing patentability under Articles 52 to 57 EPC.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practitioners should not rely on Article 69 or its Protocol as the legal basis for claim interpretation when assessing patentability in pre‑grant examinations or opposition procedures, because those provisions are directed at defining protection scope for infringement matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Article 84 EPC is a formal/technical provision and not itself a definitive basis for patentability
rubrics_metrics.description: Article 84 EPC is found under 'Filing and requirements' and thus, having a formal and technical nature, also does not provide a definitive basis for patentability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While Article 84 requires claims to be clear, concise and supported by the description, it should not be treated as the sole or controlling legal basis for interpreting claims in patentability assessments (even though case law has sometimes applied it that way).

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims must be clear, concise and supported by the description (Article 84 substantive requirement)
rubrics_metrics.description: The claims shall define the matter for which protection is sought. They shall be clear and concise and be supported by the description.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Despite the Enlarged Board's position that Article 84 is formally categorised, the substantive requirement remains relevant for drafting: ensure claims are clear and supported by the description. Previously some EPO practice emphasised that claims should be clear 'in their own right', but G1/24 requires consulting description regardless of apparent clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definitions in the description are relevant but do not automatically override claim wording; discrepancy rules unresolved
rubrics_metrics.description: A definition or similar information on a term used in the claims which is explicitly given in the description may be consulted, but the Decision does not require that the description define, or overrule, the interpretation of the claims; there is no explicit teaching in the event of a discrepancy between the claims and description.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When the description contains an explicit definition (e.g., industry vs. specification-specific meaning), that definition must be considered in interpretation, but G1/24 stops short of saying the description always controls. Practitioners should be cautious: the Decision leaves open how to resolve direct conflicts between claim wording and descriptive definitions (illustrated by the 'gathered sheet' issue in T439/22).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior case law applying Articles 69 and 84 still informs interpretive principles
rubrics_metrics.description: Even though Articles 69 and 84 are not strictly provisions on patentability, previous case law has applied them in patentability contexts and thereby established principles for claim interpretation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical EPO case law remains relevant as a source of interpretive practice; G1/24 recognises these principles even while clarifying the proper legal basis. Counsel should be mindful of both the statutory location of provisions and the body of precedent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Harmonisation with national courts and the UPC is a guiding objective
rubrics_metrics.description: The Enlarged Board noted the second principle (always consult description and drawings) is consistent with the practice of national courts of EPC states and of the Unified Patent Court (UPC), and adopted this to follow the EPC's 'harmonisation philosophy'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect increased alignment between EPO pre‑grant/opposition interpretation and national/UPC infringement interpretations, which should reduce cross‑proceeding inconsistencies. Parties should anticipate more uniform interpretive outcomes and may cite UPC/national practice as supportive authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decision raises unresolved practical issues regarding 'boilerplate' and unclaimed embodiments
rubrics_metrics.description: While G1/24 confirms always consulting the description, it does not address — and in fact raises further questions for — the extent to which the description must conform with the claims, for example as regards 'boilerplate' language and unclaimed embodiments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Drafters should take care with broad or boilerplate disclosure and unclaimed embodiments because consulting the description could expand claim interpretation; however, the exact limits (when such disclosure will be read into claims or be disregarded) remain uncertain and will require further case law.
